title: Three cards, three questions
subtitle: Reading a model card before we build
cover_prompt: Podcast cover art, flat vector illustration: two microphones facing each other over a stack of three glowing cards, soft teal and coral palette, bold simple shapes, no text

segments.title: Why read a card
segments.image_prompt: Flat vector illustration of three glowing cards fanned out beside a microphone on a desk, soft teal and coral palette, calm studio, no text

lines.text: Welcome back. Today we're reading model cards, the page that tells us what a model is for, what it costs, and where it stops.
And we're doing it with three real cards: the ones for the models that are making this very episode.
That's right. MAI-Voice-2.1 is speaking, MAI-Transcribe-2 will check our words, and MAI-Image-2.6-Flash drew the pictures.
For each card we'll ask one question, and then act on the answer. Let's start with the voice.

segments.title: The voice card: limits and access
segments.image_prompt: Flat vector illustration of a microphone emitting layered sound waves that turn into small ribbons, soft teal and coral palette, no text

lines.text: The first thing I look for is limits. The Voice card says each generation runs up to about 45 seconds, with longer audio handled by chunking.
So we didn't hand it one long script. We split every host turn into short lines, and the notebook checks that each clip stays under that limit.
The card lists the price as $22 per 1M characters, so we can count our characters and know the cost before we synthesize anything.
And a caution. The card describes instant voice cloning from a short audio clip, and it says access requires Microsoft approval and guardrails are in place to avoid misuse.
So we only use the prebuilt voices, Harper and Grant, and nothing in this episode is cloned.
One more line I underline: synthetic voices can be misused for impersonation, misinformation, or deceptive content.
That's why the player labels this audio as generated.

segments.title: The transcription card: what we can ask for
segments.image_prompt: Flat vector illustration of an audio waveform flowing into rows of small dots and dashes like captions, soft teal and coral palette, no text

lines.text: Second card, MAI-Transcribe-2. The question here is what we can ask it to return.
Word-level timestamps, according to the card, give precise timing for every word.
That's how our captions can follow along.
It also supports keyword biasing for domain-specific terms.
Our model names are exactly that, so we hand it a phrase list.
And the card describes a clean style that removes disfluencies for readable captions, notes, and published transcripts.
Watch the price line, though. It says early-bird pricing of $0.10 per hour of audio.
Early-bird suggests it may change, so we check before budgeting.
The input limits are practical too: WAV, MP3, or FLAC, up to 300 MB or 2 hours.

segments.title: The image card: what the card leaves out
segments.image_prompt: Flat vector illustration of a picture frame showing a mountain lake, with a small ruler along its edge, soft teal and coral palette, no text

lines.text: Third card, MAI-Image-2.6-Flash. Here the price line doesn't give a number. It says pricing is based on deployment type and tokens used.
So we read the token count from each response, and do the math once we have the current rate.
The card also caps output at 2,359,296 pixels, which is 1536 by 1536.
Language matters too. English is the primary language, and text rendering inside images is optimized for English.
And look at the lifecycle label. This one is a preview.
Here's my favorite part. Under known limitations, the card says the provider has not supplied this information.
When a card is silent, that's our cue to test it ourselves. So we keep the images simple, and we don't ask for any text in them.

segments.title: What we check before we build
segments.image_prompt: Flat vector illustration of a clipboard with six simple check marks beside a magnifying glass, soft teal and coral palette, no text

lines.text: So what do we check before we build? One, what it's for. Two, the limits. Three, the price, and whether it's temporary. Four, the lifecycle label. Five, access and regions.
And six, what the card doesn't say. Those gaps are where our own tests go.
That's the episode. Every claim we cited came from a card, and we checked each one before we recorded it.
Thanks for listening. See you next time.
